1.pericope_label: Again the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; I was jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I was jealous for her with great fury. Thus saith the Lord; I am returned unto Zion, and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem: and Jerusalem shall be called a city of truth; and the mountain of the Lord of hosts the holy mountain. Thus saith the Lord of hosts; There shall yet old men and old women dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and every man with his staff in his hand for very age. And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof.

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the tense of the jealousy verbs to the present and glosses the city of truth as the place where fidelity towards God has its home; Keil and Delitzsch set out the architecture of the chapter as the second half of the Lord's answer about the fasts, divided into two words of God with seven sayings and three, and quote an ancient writer for why the formula is repeated before each.

Gill notes the unique textual omission at the opening and the comfort it answers, records the Targum's future rendering of the returning, and reads the children in the streets both literally and as new-born babes of grace; Calvin rejects the reading that makes the jealousy a husband's reproach of an unfaithful wife, on the ground that the verb as construed here must be taken in a good sense of concern.

Clarke gives the chapter's outline, reports both referents of the jealousy without deciding, and argues from the children's play that such playfulness cannot be sinful since children can take exercise no other way; Wesley holds the jealousy and the fury together and supplies the contrast that war and famine had formerly cut men off before old age.

Henry reads the jealousy as one passion turned about, the wrath once against Zion now against her adversaries, and observes that Zion's own sins were her worst enemies, so that the first act of this jealousy is to take them away.

debates.question: Is the jealousy of the second verse reproach or protection?

positions.position: Not reproach: the verb as construed with its preposition must be taken in a good sense of concern, so the word means the care God had for his church.
Either: some refer it to the Jews punished as an unfaithful wife, others to enemies who exceeded their commission.
Both at once: care that she should not sin against his love, and anger against her enemies.
One passion turned about, the wrath formerly against her now against her adversaries.

debates.question: How is the promise of the restored city to be taken?

positions.position: Literally of the rebuilt city, and forward to the incarnation and a later conversion.
Literally: the temple and city rebuilt, and truth dwelling in them instead of profligacy.
Zion returning to her former condition of faithfulness and consequent favour.

outliers.claim: Turns the children playing in the streets into an argument that play is innocent: their gambols are a means of health and a proof of happiness, and since children cannot take exercise except by way of play, such playfulness cannot be sinful provided they are kept from evil words and scurrility.

themes: Again the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying,
Thus saith the Lord of hosts; I was jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I was jealous for her with great fury.
Thus saith the Lord; I am returned unto Zion, and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem: and Jerusalem shall be called a city of truth; and the mountain of the Lord of hosts the holy mountain.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts; There shall yet old men and old women dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and every man with his staff in his hand for very age.
And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof.

6.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; If it be marvellous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in these days, should it also be marvellous in mine eyes? saith the Lord of hosts. Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will save my people from the east country, and from the west country; And I will bring them, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.

schools.summary: Ellicott adjusts the tenses of the question about what is marvellous and sets beside it the saying that what is impossible with men is possible with God, and notes that Jews were in exile westward as well as eastward; Keil and Delitzsch make the grammar of the question explicit and distinguish the return under the first governor from a deliverance out of all countries which is still future and effected through the Messiah.

Gill remarks that the introductory formula is repeated for confirmation at every consolatory promise and takes the bringing as a bringing into the church and the gospel fold, where there may be one fold for Jew and Gentile.

Clarke supplies the objection the question answers and takes the gathering for every land in which any may be found, referring the promise principally to the Christian church; Wesley keeps the east country nearest home and divides the closing pair of words between God's part and theirs.

debates.question: How far does the gathering from east and west extend?

positions.position: To the two eastern powers then masters of Babylon.
To exiles in the west as well as the east, a very general dispersion being almost implied.
To every land where any are found, the promise regarding principally the Christian church and the bringing in of the Gentiles.
The return under the first governor began it, but deliverance out of all the countries of the earth is still future and comes through the Messiah.

debates.question: What force has the question about what is marvellous?

positions.position: A question expecting a negative answer, assuring both the greatness of the salvation and the certainty of its coming.
Better rendered as a past concession with a future question: though it was marvellous to them, it will not therefore be marvellous to God.
A retort to the objection that the thing is impossible in their low condition.

outliers.claim: Argues that the later deliverance is effected through the Messiah, taking this to be indisputable from the promise to bring them to Jerusalem, since the earthly city cannot be what is meant.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; If it be marvellous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in these days, should it also be marvellous in mine eyes? saith the Lord of hosts.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Behold, I will save my people from the east country, and from the west country;
And I will bring them, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.

9.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Let your hands be strong, ye that hear in these days these words by the mouth of the prophets, which were in the day that the foundation of the house of the Lord of hosts was laid, that the temple might be built. For before these days there was no hire for man, nor any hire for beast; neither was there any peace to him that went out or came in because of the affliction: for I set all men every one against his neighbour. But now I will not be unto the residue of this people as in the former days, saith the Lord of hosts. For the seed shall be prosperous; the vine shall give her fruit, and the ground shall give her increase, and the heavens shall give their dew; and I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things. And it shall come to pass, that as ye were a curse among the heathen, O house of Judah, and house of Israel; so will I save you, and ye shall be a blessing: fear not, but let your hands be strong.

schools.summary: Ellicott doubts that only two prophets are meant, distinguishes the resumption of the building from the original laying of the foundation sixteen years earlier and defends the received preposition against the old Greek, adds a Persian expedition against Egypt as a cause of the distress, and prefers the marginal seed of peace, identifying it with the vine; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same identification and reject the alternative ground for it.

Gill takes the call to strong hands of those going on with the temple, which he treats as a type of the church, reads the prosperous seed plainly, and applies the reversed curse to believers reproached by the world.

Clarke dates the founding two years before the discourse, describes the preceding years as civil divisions and domestic broils with the people abandoned to their own ways, and promises that the reversal will be complete when the Jews acknowledge their Messiah; Wesley numbers the barren period at eighteen years and names the two prophets.

Henry restricts the encouragement to those who obeyed the prophets and worked in earnest, and draws the rule that only those employed for God may expect encouragement, and that men who avoid their fathers' faults have the entail of a curse turned into a blessing.

debates.question: Which laying of the foundation is referred to?

positions.position: The one about two years before this discourse, in the fourth year of the Persian king.
The resumption of building, not the original laying sixteen years earlier, which could hardly be described as done so that the temple might be built when work was then suspended.

debates.question: What is the seed that shall be prosperous?

positions.position: The seed sown, springing up and yielding a large increase where before much sowing came to little.
The seed of peace, that is the vine, so called because it can flourish only in peaceful times.

outliers.claim: Supplies a political cause of the distress that nobody else mentions: besides the neighbouring adversaries there fell in that period a Persian expedition against Egypt, whose armies marching south through the country must have caused much distress to a people in narrow circumstances.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Let your hands be strong, ye that hear in these days these words by the mouth of the prophets, which were in the day that the foundation of the house of the Lord of hosts was laid, that the temple might be built.

For before these days there was no hire for man, nor any hire for beast; neither was there any peace to him that went out or came in because of the affliction: for I set all men every one against his neighbour.
But now I will not be unto the residue of this people as in the former days, saith the Lord of hosts.

For the seed shall be prosperous; the vine shall give her fruit, and the ground shall give her increase, and the heavens shall give their dew; and I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things.
And it shall come to pass, that as ye were a curse among the heathen, O house of Judah, and house of Israel; so will I save you, and ye shall be a blessing: fear not, but let your hands be strong.

14.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord of hosts; As I thought to punish you, when your fathers provoked me to wrath, saith the Lord of hosts, and I repented not: So again have I thought in these days to do well unto Jerusalem and to the house of Judah: fear ye not. These are the things that ye shall do; Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates: And let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour; and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith the Lord. And the word of the Lord of hosts came unto me, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful feasts; therefore love the truth and peace.

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the judgment of truth and peace as given according to the true facts and tending to peace between man and man, and records that the old Greek renders the fasts by ordinal rather than by month; Keil and Delitzsch describe the ground and condition of the promise formally and identify the closing word of God as the direct answer to the inquiry about the fasts.

Gill observes that God confirms his promise by pointing to the fulfilment of his threatening, takes the required duties as obligations of gratitude, remarks that hatred without a cause was a governing vice under the second temple, and marks the new prophecy about the abrogation of the fasts and the calling of the Gentiles.

Clarke refers the required duties back to the previous chapter and gives each of the four fasts its historical occasion; Wesley glosses the clause about not repenting, locates the gates as the seat of judicature, and makes the turning of the fasts conditional on the duties being done.

Henry distinguishes those who fasted in hypocrisy from those who humbled themselves in sincerity, states the rule that joyous times come to the church after troublous ones, and presses the appended exhortation to love truth and peace even where honesty costs the gains others get dishonestly.

debates.question: Is the turning of the fasts into feasts conditional?

positions.position: Yes: the verse decides the case provided the duties just required are done.
The condition attaches to the whole promise, the preceding verses giving its ground and these its condition.
The assurance belongs to those who humbled themselves in sincerity, those who fasted in hypocrisy having had their doom already.

debates.question: What occasions did the four fasts commemorate?

positions.position: The taking of the city, the ruin of the temple, the murder of the governor, and the beginning of the siege.
The old Greek names them by ordinal rather than by month, the fourth fast rather than the fast of the fourth.

outliers.claim: States the rule that joyous times come to the church after troublous ones, and that if weeping endures more than a night and joy does not come the next morning, the morning that introduces it will come at length.

themes: For thus saith the Lord of hosts; As I thought to punish you, when your fathers provoked me to wrath, saith the Lord of hosts, and I repented not:
So again have I thought in these days to do well unto Jerusalem and to the house of Judah: fear ye not.
These are the things that ye shall do; Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates:
And let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour; and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith the Lord.
And the word of the Lord of hosts came unto me, saying,

Thus saith the Lord of hosts; The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful feasts; therefore love the truth and peace.

20.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; It shall yet come to pass, that there shall come people, and the inhabitants of many cities: And the inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, Let us go speedily to pray before the Lord, and to seek the Lord of hosts: I will go also. Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts; In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.

schools.summary: Ellicott records the old Greek's reading that the inhabitants of five cities come together to one, borrowing the number perhaps from another prophet, and says the ten men are an indefinite number for a large one; Keil and Delitzsch treat these verses as no new promise but an indication of the magnitude of the salvation already appointed, and describe the heathen crowding to Israel to be received into fellowship as a nation.

Gill reads the mutual invitation as evidence of concern for one another's spiritual welfare and of readiness to attend worship, and takes the strong nations for mighty kingdoms which have professed Christianity since the downfall of paganism.

Clarke turns the answering clause into an exhortation to go speedily, suggests the Mohammedan tribes and the peoples of Egypt and Syria as the strong nations, and reads the ten men first as a proportion and then as a large number, drawing the inference that converted Jews should be the instruments of converting Gentiles; Wesley makes the ten mean many, notes that no nation is any longer excluded, and keeps a literal and a mystical sense of the city.

debates.question: Who are the many people and strong nations?

positions.position: Mighty kingdoms which have professed Christianity since the downfall of paganism.
Perhaps the Mohammedan tribes near Palestine, and the peoples of Egypt, of the rocky country and of Syria.
The first-fruits are the peoples present at Pentecost; mystically the city is the church.
The heathen crowding to Israel and Judah to be received into fellowship with them as a nation.

debates.question: What does the number ten signify?

positions.position: A proportion of converts to Jews as ten to one, though it may simply mean a great number without comparison.
An indefinite number for a large one, as seven is used elsewhere.

outliers.claim: Observes that catching hold of the skirt is a gesture naturally used to entreat assistance and protection, and relays another scholar's account that these four verses cover the converts received between the captivity and the coming of Christ, the disciples the Jewish preachers afterwards made, and future conversions of which the restoration of the Jews will be an eminent cause.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts; It shall yet come to pass, that there shall come people, and the inhabitants of many cities:
And the inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, Let us go speedily to pray before the Lord, and to seek the Lord of hosts: I will go also.
Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the Lord.

Thus saith the Lord of hosts; In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.
